newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Shell Nigeria loses $289 million to oil spills.
newsitem.headline: Shell Nigeria loses $289 million to oil spills.

text.p: The Nigerian unit of Royal Dutch Shell Group lost $289 million in 1996 from 215 oil spills in the Niger Delta, the independent Thisday newspaper reported on Wednesday.

It quoted Paul Morgan, Shell Nigeria's head of society and environment, as saying the spills, the equivalent of 34,000 barrels of crude oil, occurred as a result of sabotage and cost the company an average of $8,500 on land and $22,500 in swamps to clean up.

He said most of the spills occurred on land, and "have always been discovered to be the deliberate attempts of saboteurs, whose motives range from seeking to benefit from the economic advantage of a clean up exercise thereafter or out of frustration."
After such incidents prompt salvage operations were often delayed by host communities that barricade the spill sites in order to establish their claims for compensation, he said.

Morgan had taken a team of local reporters to spill sites in the upper Niger Delta where holes had been bored in pipelines in what he called "12 O'clock, 3 O'clock and 9 O'clock positions" which were not the usual positions for corrosions and leakages.

There has been growing restiveness in the Niger Delta, Nigeria's main oil producing region, among communities that feel they have been denied the benefits of oil production going on in their backyards.

Hubert Nwokolo, Shell Nigeria's eastern division operations manager, was quoted as enumerating Shell's work for local communities "and all that they are asking from us are things that the government is obliged to do, yet we even do them in the face of a drastically reduced budget".
According to him, the company has the latest equipment for cleaning oil spills in Nigeria and in addition retains the services of a British expert in case of major spills.
